stop 2 card 6, answer 2: copies a Prep line word for word

explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, “Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.” (Galatians 5:1) Christ has set them free, so they hold on to that freedom with both hands. Think of a full cookie tray: you grab it firm, and you don't let it wobble.

explanations.answer: Work hard to earn their freedom
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul never tells them to work for freedom. He says, “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free.” (Galatians 5:1) Freedom is a gift that's already been given, not a paycheck. What Paul asks is that they stand firm in it.

Not quite, baker. Paul doesn't tell them to hush up. He tells them to stand firm (Galatians 5:1), which is the opposite of sitting quietly in the corner. Freedom is something you hold up where people can see it.

That's the one, baker. Paul warns them, “do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.” (Galatians 5:1) He's serious about that warning. I know a heavy load when I feel one, since I spent years under takeout menus in a junk drawer.

Not quite, friend. Paul does warn them, and the words are right there: “do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.” (Galatians 5:1) He isn't saying they can take on whatever load they like. He wants them to stay out from under that yoke.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “Take notice: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all.” (Galatians 5:2) He signs his own name to it, so listen up. Papa Dorin always puts down his spatula when somebody signs their name like that.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the opposite. If they let themselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to them at all (Galatians 5:2). He doesn't add value here. He takes it away, and that's a hard thing to hear.
Not quite, baker. Paul doesn't say Christ stays the same. He says Christ will be of no value to them at all (Galatians 5:2). That's a big drop, and Paul isn't being gentle about it.

Not quite, friend. Paul says something bigger than that. He writes, “Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law.” (Galatians 5:3) It's the whole law, not just one command.

You got it, baker. Paul says the man is obligated to obey the whole law, not just one command. “Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law.” (Galatians 5:3) That's a load much bigger than one little chore.

explanations.answer: They have been severed from Christ
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul writes, “You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.” (Galatians 5:4) Those are strong words, and Paul means every one of them. He's talking about people trying to be justified by the law, and he says they've been cut off from Christ.

explanations.answer: They have drawn closer to Christ
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Paul says the opposite. Those trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ (Galatians 5:4). They've moved away from Him, not closer.
Not quite, friend. Verse 4 says they have fallen away from grace (Galatians 5:4). Grace isn't something you pile on like extra chocolate chips. Paul says these people have fallen away from it.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness.” (Galatians 5:5) Faith is what they lean on while they wait, the way I wait by the oven for the timer. The waiting is eager, and the faith is what carries it.

Not quite, friend. The law is what some are trying to be justified by, and Paul warns them off that road (Galatians 5:4). In verse 5, the hope is awaited by faith through the Spirit, so the blank needs faith, not law.
Not quite, baker. Paul says “by faith” and “through the Spirit” (Galatians 5:5), not effort. Eager waiting in faith is what he has in mind, and nobody earns it by trying harder.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “What matters is faith expressing itself through love.” (Galatians 5:6) Circumcision doesn't count, and neither does being uncircumcised. The faith that comes out in love is the batch that matters.

Not quite, friend. Paul says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value in Christ Jesus (Galatians 5:6). Keeping every command perfectly isn't the thing he names. He says faith expressing itself through love is what matters.

explanations.answer: Coming from the right family line
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Verse 6 says nothing about family lines. It names circumcision and uncircumcision as having no value in Christ Jesus, and then names faith working through love as what matters (Galatians 5:6).

Not quite, friend. Paul says, “Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you.” (Galatians 5:8) He says it outright. The persuasion slowing them down doesn't come from the One who called them.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you.” (Galatians 5:8) He doesn't leave it to guessing. The persuasion that's slowing the Galatians down doesn't come from the One who called them.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough.” (Galatians 5:9) One small bit spreads through everything it touches. That's why I keep an eye on every batch, start to finish.
Not quite, friend. Paul says the leaven works through the whole batch, not just the top (Galatians 5:9). A little bit gets in and spreads all the way through.
Not quite, baker. The spot it touches is only where it starts. Paul says it works through the whole batch of dough (Galatians 5:9), so it doesn't stop at the first spot.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “I am confident in the Lord that you will take no other view. The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.” (Galatians 5:10) He doesn't name the troublemaker. He says that person will carry the judgment, and Paul is confident of it.

explanations.answer: He will be let off free
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul says the one troubling them will bear the judgment (Galatians 5:10). Going free isn't what the verse says. Paul is confident the Lord will deal with that person.

explanations.answer: He will be put in charge
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The verse talks about judgment, not leadership. Paul writes that the one troubling them will bear the judgment (Galatians 5:10), and that's the outcome he expects.

Not quite, friend. Paul asks, “if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” (Galatians 5:11) He's raising the question, not confessing to it. The “if” is how he sets up what he's answering.

You got it, baker. Paul asks, “if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” (Galatians 5:11) That “if” is a question he's raising. Then he says, “In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished,” which shows where that road would lead.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” (Galatians 5:13) He celebrates their freedom and warns them not to waste it. Freedom is a gift, and it's easy to waste a gift.

Not quite, friend. Paul says they were called to freedom, and then he warns them not to use it as an opportunity for the flesh (Galatians 5:13). The warning is right there in the verse, in his own words.

You got it, baker. Paul writes, “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”” (Galatians 5:14) The whole law sums up in one line. Papa Dorin loves a short recipe like that, where one line says it all.
Not quite, friend. Paul doesn't name the Sabbath here. He says the entire law is fulfilled in a single decree, and that decree is “Love your neighbor as yourself.” (Galatians 5:14)
Not quite, baker. Paul doesn't name that command either. He points to one decree as the place the whole law is fulfilled: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” (Galatians 5:14)

You got it, baker. Paul warns, “But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another.” (Galatians 5:15) That's a serious warning about turning on each other. Paul wants them to watch out for it.

Not quite, friend. Paul doesn't warn about being scattered. He says that if they keep biting and devouring one another, they will be consumed by one another (Galatians 5:15). Consumed is the word he uses.
Not quite, baker. The verse doesn't mention shame. It warns that they will be consumed by one another if they keep biting and devouring each other (Galatians 5:15), so consumed is the word that fits.
